strengths: The motivation is relevant: individual benefits can depend on neighboring activations, so maximizing influence spread need not maximize total benefit.
Combining hypergraph interference estimation with seed selection is a potentially useful research direction. Providing greedy and accelerated variants addresses an important computational challenge.

The paper includes four datasets, pseudocode, extensive appendices, and a code link. G-CauIM improves the reported metric across all four datasets, while A-CauIM reports substantial runtime reductions.
weaknesses: The central guarantee in Theorem 4.4 is false for the stated dynamic-gain model. Consider zero propagation and budget two: nodes a and b each have gain 1 unless the other is activated, when their gain becomes 100; node c has constant gain 2. All gains are positive and bounded, but greedy selects c first and obtains 3, versus the optimum of 200. Appendix F treats gains as fixed and omits their changes with activation. Independently, Eq. (15) incorrectly bounds the accumulated error: at K=15, its coefficient is approximately 5.329, whereas the proposed upper bound is 0.393. These are fundamental failures in the main theoretical contribution.

The activation probabilities and objective are inconsistent. Section 2 defines activation probability as the sum of per-seed reachability probabilities, which double-counts overlapping reachability and can exceed one. Moreover, E[ap(i;S) tau_i] generally differs from E[T_i tau_i] when effects depend on correlated neighboring activations. Consequently, the objective preceding Eq. (2) does not generally equal the realized active-node reward used in the Monte Carlo algorithm.

Causal identification is not established. Assumption 2.2 states independence between the two potential outcomes conditional on treatment and environment; this is not the treatment–potential-outcome exchangeability condition needed for the identification formula in footnote 5. Treatment/exposure overlap and support under seed-induced activation distributions are also unaddressed. Thus, fitting the proposed predictor does not establish recovery of causal effects.

A-CauIM introduces unvalidated approximations to diffusion, random environments, and discrete marginal gains in Eqs. (4)–(5). There is neither an approximation bound nor targeted empirical validation connecting its derivative score to actual seed-addition gains. Even corrected exact-greedy guarantees would not automatically apply. Initialization, preservation of seed activation, convergence criteria, and the iteration dependence of the claimed complexity require clarification.

The experiments do not independently validate causal benefit. Appendix C describes simulated treatments/effects on real network topologies, while evaluation uses the same trained ITE estimator used for optimization. No true-effect accuracy or independent evaluation against the simulated reward is reported. Comparisons include only random selection and one greedy baseline, without key component ablations or uncertainty intervals in Table 1. A-CauIM also underperforms the baseline on Contact, 66.78 versus 68.12. These results provide insufficient support for the broad effectiveness, robustness, and comparative efficiency claims.

Reproducibility and positioning remain incomplete despite the code link. Important specifications include the exact outcome generator, graph sizes and preprocessing, network/training hyperparameters, M/C/Cd, and hardware and training-cost accounting for timing. The baseline's treatment of ITE is ambiguous. The relationship to the cited work on causal intervention-policy enhancement [37] also needs a precise comparison to establish the new technical contribution.
